title: R’ Abba (without a patronymic)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: R’ Abba (without a patronymic). We find several sages bearing this name at different times. The learned author of Mishpechot Soferim counted seven sages called simply R’ Abba, from the end of the tannaitic period until the days of Rav Ashi. In truth, however, there were only three, and all of them were amoraim.[^1]

For what we find in the Mekhilta, Beshalach, at the beginning of the section Vayassa—“R’ Abba said: Our holy teacher told me this matter: There was a man in the land of Israel whom they called Merutah,” etc.—also appears in Shemot Rabbah 24:4. (“Akiva” in the Mekhilta is a scribal error.) In the old Tanchuma, Beshalach 18, the reading is “R’ Acha said”; in R. Shlomo Buber’s Tanchuma, the reading is “Rabbi Chiyya the Great.” This is a scribal error, since Rabbi Chiyya did not go down to Babylonia after he had gone up to the land of Israel. It seems clear that the correct reading is Rav Abba: he is “Rav,” whose name was Abba. We may rely on the testimony of Rav Hai Gaon, cited in the Arukh under the entry Rav, that Rav is mentioned in three places as “Rav Abba,” all of them baraitot: (1) Berakhot 49a: “Rav Abba says: He must mention thanksgiving.” (2) Shabbat 135b: “Rav Abba says: He immersed her and afterward she gave birth”—our reading is R’ Chama. (3) Ketubot 81a: “R’ Abba said: I asked Sumchus.” Thus, without doubt, the R’ Abba mentioned in the Mekhilta together with our holy teacher is also Rav.[^2]

As for the baraita in Yevamot 121b, “R’ Abba said: Nevertheless, his son died of thirst,” the name there should read R’ Acha, as in Bava Kamma 50a. So it also reads in Shekalim 5:1 and in Dikdukei Soferim. Likewise, what we find in Tosefta Beitzah, chapter 1, and Chullin, chapter 4—“R’ Abba said: This is one of the things concerning which Rabbi Chiyya would say, ‘I have no answer,’ and Rabbi Eleazar HaKappar Beribbi supplied an answer”—undoubtedly also refers to Rav. The statement is brought in Tosefta Chullin, chapter 6, where the reading has become corrupt. It is also brought in Yerushalmi Beitzah 3:3, where it reads “R’ Avin said”; it should read “R’ Abba said.”

As for the old Midrash Tehillim, chapter 4, which has “R’ Kohen in the name of R’ Abba,” R. Shlomo Buber has already emended it there, in note 9, to “R’ Natan in the name of R’ Acha.” And where Shir HaShirim Rabbah, chapter 4, on the verse “With me from Lebanon,” has “Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosi in the name of R’ Abba,” this is a scribal error: it should read “in the name of his father,” for the statement derives from the source cited as מט״ע רבה, chapter 23, where it is Rabbi Yosi’s.[^3] We have thus succeeded in establishing that an unspecified R’ Abba mentioned in the tannaitic period is Rav, of whom they said, “Rav is a tanna and may disagree.”

The same applies to the R’ Abba mentioned in Seder Tannaim VeAmoraim and in Sefer HaKeritot, Yemot Olam, gate 2. This is its wording: “When Rav came to Babylonia in the year הק״ל of the Era of Documents, he found R’ Abba exercising authority in Babylonia. As long as R’ Abba lived, Rav did not exercise authority, until R’ Abba died.” Sefer Yuchasin correctly understood this R’ Abba to be Abba bar Avuha diShmuel, for he was indeed the head and leader of Babylonia as a whole. Although his son Shmuel was already head of the academy in Nehardea during his father’s lifetime, and Rav was in Sura, the supreme authority remained in the hands of Shmuel’s father, as explained in his entry. This is what the author of Sefer HaKeritot meant.[^4]

The author of Mishpechot Soferim brings an “R’ Abba,” an amora in the land of Israel, who learned laws directly from our holy teacher. His evidence is Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:2: “R’ Acha, R’ Ba in the name of ‘Rabbi’: once he washes his hands.” In fact, this is a scribal error and should read “in the name of Rav,” for Shabbat 9b states explicitly: “When is the beginning of a meal? Rav says: Once he washes his hands.”

He also brings the passage in Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 18: “R’ Abba said: Even about this he need not have raised the difficulty, for Rabbi was sitting and expounding, and did they not say to Abba Yudan, his interpreter,” etc. Here, without doubt, Rabbi means our holy teacher, for it is well known that Abba Yudan was his interpreter. But the aforementioned scholar failed to notice that a scribal error had entered Midrash Rabbah. The original is in Yerushalmi Berakhot 4:1, 28b, where the correct reading is: “R’ Assi said: Rabbi Yochanan disagrees—and even about that he need not have disagreed, for he used to instruct your father,” etc.[^5]

He likewise says that this R’ Abba received teachings directly from Rabbi’s disciples: from Rabbi Chanina in Ketubot 88b, “R’ Abba said in the name of Rabbi Chanina.” But Shittah Mekubbetzet has already deleted the words “R’ Abba.” Dikdukei Soferim likewise reports that all the manuscripts lack the words “R’ Abba.”

As for Ketubot 1:4, “R’ Abba in the name of Rabbi Yannai,” this statement is in fact brought in Ketubot 16a simply in the name of Rabbi Yannai. And Sanhedrin 3:8—“R’ Berekhya, R’ Chelbo, R’ Ba in the name of Rabbi Yannai”—is also no proof, since an intervening amora is undoubtedly missing, as in Ketubot 72a: “R’ Abba said in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya, who said in the name of Rabbi Yannai.” In Nedarim 22a, R’ Abba merely explains Rabbi Yannai’s words.

He also says that we find him together with Rabbi Yonatan, as in Vayikra Rabbah 22:9: “R’ Abba and Rabbi Yonatan say in the name of R’ Levi.” It is astonishing that he did not notice that a scribal error had entered the passage. How could Rabbi Yonatan speak in the name of R’ Levi, who was a preacher in Rabbi Yochanan’s academy? The reading of Yalkut on Psalms 146, however, is “R’ Acha and Rav Biyona in the name of Rabbi Meir.”

He likewise says that this was the R’ Abba to whom Resh Lakish addressed a question and who answered him, as in Yerushalmi Nedarim 1:2. The author of Mevo HaYerushalmi has already noted, under R’ Ba, that this is a scribal error. It is plausible that the meaning is: “Resh Lakish be‘a qomei R’ Ba”—that is, R’ Ba asked Resh Lakish.[^6]
It therefore seems clear that there were only three sages called simply R’ Abba. We shall explain them in chronological order.

notes.text: “Without a patronymic” renders סתם: occurrences that name Abba without identifying which sage is intended. The count of three, the proposed identifications and the textual emendations below are Hyman’s argument.

“Our holy teacher” is Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi. A baraita is a tannaitic teaching outside the Mishnah. In the Shabbat quotation, the feminine pronouns are retained: the formulation concerns immersion before giving birth, rather than immersion of the newborn afterward.
The abbreviated source title מט״ע רבה is retained as printed; its expansion is uncertain. Hyman contrasts “Abba” with אביו, “his father,” identifying the latter as Rabbi Yosi.

The year is printed הק״ל in the Era of Documents; its numerical interpretation is uncertain. “Abba bar Avuha diShmuel” is Hyman’s designation for Shmuel’s father. His distinction here is between leadership of the individual academies and authority over Babylonia as a whole.

אמורא here means the public interpreter or spokesman, rather than a member of the historical class of amoraim. Hyman first explains why the wording in Bereishit Rabbah suggests Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, then argues for a different reading from the Yerushalmi.

The quoted Aramaic appears to make Resh Lakish the questioner; Hyman’s explanation reverses the direction and makes R’ Ba the questioner. Both the wording and his proposed interpretation are retained.
